question: How do we know the Earth is old?
hook: In 1862 Lord Kelvin, the leading physicist of his day, calculated from the Earth's cooling that it was somewhere between 20 and 400 million years old. The figure accepted today, about 4.54 billion years, came from a process nobody knew existed until 1896: radioactivity.

steps.note: Steno's rules of superposition and cross-cutting let you put rocks in order, the first step to any history of the Earth.
Seeing how sediment settles and hardens into stone shows why thick stacks of layers imply long spans of time.
Hutton's unconformity at Siccar Point and the mile of rock in the Grand Canyon are where geologists first felt the depth of time.
Fossils are dated by the rocks that hold them, and they also reveal that the layers record a long succession of vanished worlds.
The geological time scale turns layers and index fossils into a relative calendar, still without numbers attached.
Darwin's theory needed enormous stretches of time for selection to work, so biology put pressure on geology to find them.
Kelvin's short age came from treating the Earth as a hot body losing heat by conduction; this is the physics he used, and it was sound.
Radioactive decay is the missing piece: it quietly heats the Earth's interior and ticks at a fixed rate set by the half-life.
Uranium-lead dating of zircons and meteorites turns decay into ages in years, giving the 4.5 billion-year figure.
Plates moving a few centimetres a year needed some 200 million years to open the Atlantic, an independent check on deep time.
Kelvin also argued that gravity could power the Sun for only tens of millions of years; nuclear fusion removes that limit and makes the Sun a middle-aged star.
With the clock calibrated, the whole history of life, from 3.5 billion-year-old stromatolites onward, falls into place on one timeline.

question: Why did Europe industrialise first?
hook: By Paul Bairoch's widely cited estimates, China and India together made more than half of the world's manufactured goods around 1750. By 1880 Britain alone was making nearly a quarter.

steps.note: Start with the baseline: for millennia every economy ran on farming, trade and money, with no sustained growth anywhere.
Song and Ming China were richer and more inventive than Europe for centuries, which is exactly what makes the question hard.
The Black Death killed so many workers that survivors could demand higher wages, a shift some historians see as the long root of labour-saving invention.
Medieval Europe's heavy plough, universities and printing press show it was not standing still before the modern era.
Atlantic voyages gave Europe American silver, new crops and new land, a windfall no other region received.
Chartered joint-stock companies let merchants pool capital and run empires for profit, an institutional innovation in its own right.
Slave-grown sugar and cotton fed Europe's markets and mills, a reminder that the rise rested on coerced labour elsewhere.
The Scientific Revolution unfolded alongside the powerful Mughal, Ottoman and Ming empires, so science alone cannot be the whole answer.
The institutions argument: secure property, patents and limits on rulers may explain why ideas became investment.
Now the main event: coal near the surface, high wages, empire and a tinkering culture came together in 18th-century Britain.
Steam engines worked long before Carnot explained their limits in 1824, showing practice ran ahead of theory.
Finally, the comparison that tests every explanation: why the US, Germany and Japan followed quickly while China and India did not.

question: How does a vaccine teach your body?
hook: Edward Jenner vaccinated a boy against smallpox in 1796, about a century before anyone knew viruses existed. Smallpox, which killed an estimated 300 million people in the 20th century alone, was declared eradicated in 1980.

steps.note: Jenner's cowpox experiment shows vaccination working long before anyone could explain why.
Germ theory supplied the first half of the explanation: specific microbes cause specific diseases.
Meet the enemy: a virus is just a genome in a protein coat, with no metabolism of its own.
A virus must grip a specific receptor to get in, so its surface proteins are the natural targets for a vaccine.
Proteins fold into precise 3D shapes, and it is these shapes that the immune system learns to recognise.
Your body has a fast, generic innate defence and a slow, specific adaptive one; vaccines work on the second.
B cells sharpen their antibodies through mutation and selection, so the response a vaccine primes gets better at binding its exact target.
T cells kill infected cells and coordinate the whole response, the other half of lasting protection.
Cells turn mRNA into protein, the step an mRNA vaccine borrows to make your own cells display a harmless piece of the virus.
The vaccine types side by side, from inactivated and live attenuated to mRNA, and why some viruses still resist them.
The COVID-19 mRNA vaccines show the whole chain, from genome sequence to approved vaccine, happening within a year.
Protection spills over to people you never meet, which is why economists treat herd immunity as a public good.

question: Can a computer understand language?
hook: Large language models are trained on one simple task: predict the next piece of text. From that alone they learn to translate, summarise and argue, which makes a question John Searle posed in 1980 urgent: does following rules ever add up to understanding?

steps.note: First pin down what needs understanding: Frege's split between what a word refers to and how it presents it.
Chomsky showed language is recursive, letting finite rules produce infinitely many sentences, a hard target for any machine.
Context-free grammars are the mathematics of that recursion, and the first serious attempt to make grammar machine-readable.
Turing's universal machine shows one device can run any procedure, so if understanding is a procedure a computer could run it.
Turing's 1950 test proposes judging machine minds by conversation alone, setting the terms of the debate.
Markov chains give the simplest statistical model of text: guess the next word from the ones before it.
Modern systems turn each word into a vector, so meaning becomes position and direction in a high-dimensional space.
Neural networks learn those vectors and everything built on them by adjusting weights to reduce prediction error.
The transformer's attention lets every word look at every other word, the architectural leap behind today's language models.
Scale next-word prediction up to much of the internet and you get an LLM, including its fluency and its hallucinations.
Grice's implicatures, meaning what we do not literally say, are a demanding test of whether a system grasps intent.
Searle's Chinese Room returns the question to you: is symbol manipulation, however good, the same as understanding?

question: Why do prices rise?
hook: In the autumn of 1923, German prices were doubling every few days. In 16th-century Europe, as American silver poured in, prices rose several-fold over about a century. Both are inflation, and the explanations are closely related.

steps.note: Begin with a single price: supply and demand explain why one good gets dearer when buyers want more or sellers offer less.
Elasticity explains why some price jumps are so sharp: when people cannot do without something, a small shortage moves the price a lot.
Oil shows how a single scarce input, tangled in politics, can push up the price of almost everything at once.
To see all prices rising together, you need to see money itself as a good whose value can fall.
Silver from Potosí fed Europe's 'Price Revolution', a historical case of more money chasing the same goods.
Today most money is created by banks when they lend, so the money supply is not just coins and notes.
The core lesson: how inflation is measured, and its demand-pull, cost-push and monetary causes, up to Weimar-style hyperinflation.
Friedman's claim that inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon, and the rival schools it provoked.
Central banks are the institutions charged with keeping prices stable, and here is how they do it.
Interest rates are the main lever: the Taylor rule shows how central banks respond when prices run ahead.
Finally, why governments hand this power to independent central banks, and what it costs when politics interferes.

question: Where do words come from?
hook: No one has ever heard Proto-Indo-European spoken, and no text of it survives. Yet linguists can reconstruct its word for wheel, *kʷékʷlos, which lives on in English wheel, Greek kyklos and Sanskrit cakra.

steps.note: Words are built from smaller meaningful parts, morphemes, the raw material every word history works with.
Cognates like father, Vater and pater show that languages form families descended from a common ancestor.
Grimm's Law shows sound change is regular, which is what lets linguists trace words across thousands of years.
Applying the comparative method rebuilds Proto-Indo-European, the ancestor of half the world's languages, from its descendants alone.
Writing, invented around 3200 BCE, is when words begin leaving direct evidence of their own past.
Old English and Beowulf show the Germanic core of English before the Norman Conquest reshaped it.
Chaucer's Middle English captures the language mid-transformation, full of fresh borrowings from French.
Borrowing and semantic drift explain why so much English vocabulary is foreign and why old words mean new things.
Pidgins and creoles show entirely new languages, and their words, being born from contact within a few generations.
Compounding, blending and conversion are how new words are coined today, from sunflower to googling.
Words spread and die like replicators; Dawkins even coined 'meme' to make the point, and it caught on.

question: Is the universe made of maths?
hook: In 1928 Paul Dirac wrote down an equation for the electron that had an extra set of solutions nobody had asked for. They turned out to describe antimatter, and the positron was found in 1932.

steps.note: The Pythagoreans first claimed that all is number, and the discovery of irrational numbers promptly complicated the claim.
Euclid showed how a few axioms generate a whole geometry, and his troublesome parallel postulate will matter later.
Newton's synthesis showed that one equation governs falling apples and orbiting planets, the first great triumph of mathematical physics.
Maxwell's equations predicted waves travelling at the speed of light, so mathematics revealed what light is.
Complex numbers began as a trick for solving equations with no apparent physical meaning.
Yet the quantum wavefunction is complex-valued, and the Schrödinger equation cannot be written without i.
Groups are the mathematics of symmetry, studied for their own elegance long before physics needed them.
The particle zoo is organised by symmetry, and Dirac's equation predicted antimatter before anyone saw it.
General relativity describes gravity as curved spacetime, using geometry that grew out of doubts about Euclid's parallel postulate.
Wigner named the puzzle: why should mathematics invented for its own sake fit nature so precisely?
Platonists say mathematical objects exist independently; formalists say maths is a game with symbols. Your answer shapes your answer to the question.
The boldest version says the universe is a computation; physical limits like the Bekenstein bound show what that would demand.

question: What makes a story work?
hook: Aristotle's analysis of plot, written around 335 BCE, still underpins modern screenwriting manuals. In 1928 Vladimir Propp found that a hundred Russian fairy tales were built from just 31 recurring plot functions.

steps.note: Stories begin as myths that explain the world, so their first job was to make sense of things.
Homer's epics were composed orally and polished by generations of performers, a long test of what holds an audience.
Propp's analysis of folktales shows that stories share a hidden grammar of recurring moves.
Aristotle's Poetics gives the first theory of plot: a unified action, a flawed hero and a reversal that produces catharsis.
Why do we enjoy stories full of suffering? The paradox of tragedy asks what a story does for its audience.
Forster's test, 'the queen died of grief', shows that plot is causation, and Freytag's pyramid gives it a shape.
News writing inverts the pyramid and tells the ending first, a useful contrast that shows structure depends on purpose.
Our appetite for causal pattern is so strong that we see plots in noise, which is why a good story can feel true.
Characters we believe in, whether flat or round, are what make readers care what happens next.
Chekhov showed that restraint and suggestion can move readers more than a tidy plot.
Reader-response theory finishes the argument: a story works only when the reader fills its gaps.

question: How do we know what happened in the past?
hook: Writing is only about 5,000 years old, while our species is roughly 300,000 years old. For almost all of the human story there are no documents at all, yet we still know a great deal about it.

steps.note: Start with the standard: knowing the past means having justified true beliefs about events nobody alive witnessed.
Source criticism is the historian's core tool: who made this document, when, why, and could it be forged?
Writing began in Sumer around 3200 BCE, marking the line between history told in documents and prehistory.
Some written records stay silent because nobody can read them, and decipherment needs the right mix of language, corpus and clues.
Atlantis is a test case: a story with no material traces, and how to tell legend from lost history.
Pompeii, Angkor and Troy show how real places vanish and how texts, even Homer, can lead diggers to them.
Aerial photography, LiDAR and ground radar reveal buried sites without lifting a spade.
Superposition, deeper means older, orders archaeological layers just as it orders rocks.
Radiocarbon dating puts absolute ages on bone, wood and charcoal, calibrated against tree rings.
Göbekli Tepe, dated to about 9500 BCE, shows the evidence can overturn the textbook sequence of farming first, temples later.
Ancient DNA now reads migrations and interbreeding, such as with Neanderthals, straight from bones.
Finally, a check on over-reach: how sensational claims about the past are tested, and why most fail.
